paragraphs: Mixture models describe observations through combinations of hidden components. For interpretation, it can be useful for each observation to involve only a few components. The paper studies how to encourage that sparsity when mixture weights already have a fixed L1 norm. Under this constraint, an ordinary L1 penalty cannot distinguish sparse mixtures from more spread-out ones.

Concave regularization can encourage sparse weights, but it complicates fitting with expectation maximization. In particular, the maximization step can lose the concavity that would make it easier to handle. The authors use the Mountain Pass Theorem to establish easily checked conditions under which this step remains well behaved despite that loss. The result is conditional, rather than a guarantee for every concave penalty.

The paper also connects logarithmic regularization to a proposed pseudo-Dirichlet distribution, extending the ordinary Dirichlet distribution to better support sparsity. An application learns sparse topic mixtures from 2,406 weblogs. Together, these contributions connect an interpretable modeling preference with conditions that make its associated optimization manageable.
neurips-2011-a-concave-regularization-te.tldr: The paper gives checkable conditions that make concave sparsity penalties manageable when fitting mixture models.

paragraphs: A classification system may have many classifiers available, each contributing different information at a computational cost. Applying them through a fixed procedure can spend effort on observations that are less useful for a particular input. This paper treats classification at test time as a sequence of decisions about which classifier to consult next.

Each classifier output becomes a potential observation. A probabilistic model uses the outputs already collected to estimate how much another observation could improve classification. A value-based calculation balances this expected gain against the cost of obtaining it. Because earlier results affect later choices, different test examples can follow different paths through the same ensemble.

Experiments on real-world datasets show that this adaptive process can match or exceed the accuracy of traditional methods while using a fraction of their computation. The finding supports choosing computation separately for each instance: the useful question is not just which classifiers are available, but which one is worth running given what the system already knows.
neurips-2011-active-classification-based.tldr: An adaptive test-time procedure selects classifiers by expected benefit and cost, achieving strong accuracy with less computation in experiments.

paragraphs: Semidefinite programs are optimization problems used across machine learning and related areas. At very large data scales, even an algorithm whose running time grows linearly with the input can be expensive. This paper addresses that bottleneck by seeking approximate solutions with a running time that grows more slowly than the input size.

The authors present what they identify as the first sublinear-time approximation algorithm for semidefinite programs, together with an analysis of the algorithm. Approximation is central to the contribution: the stated result concerns obtaining an approximate answer efficiently. The paper also supplies theoretical lower bounds, placing the algorithmic development alongside results about limits on what computation can achieve.

A further contribution improves the algorithm for the particular task of supervised distance-metric learning. That specialization connects the general optimization result to a machine learning problem. The authors suggest that the approach may help when data volume makes even linear-time methods impractical; the abstract frames this practical usefulness as a possibility, rather than an experimentally established outcome.
neurips-2011-approximating-semidefinite-.tldr: The paper develops a sublinear-time approximation algorithm for semidefinite programs and an improved specialization for distance-metric learning.

paragraphs: An expert diagnosing a problem provides information through both test results and the choice of which test to run next. Selecting a test suggests that the expert considers it diagnostically valuable relative to alternatives. This paper develops a way to use those choices to refine the parameters of a Bayesian network used for diagnosis.

The authors translate consistency with the expert's selections into constraints on the network parameters. These constraints are non-convex, making parameter fitting more difficult. To incorporate them, the method adds nodes that encode constraint likelihoods. This lets information from test ordering enter the probabilistic model alongside whatever ordinary data are available.

The paper proposes Gibbs sampling, stochastic hill climbing, and greedy search approaches for finding a maximum a posteriori parameter estimate. It demonstrates the method using manufacturing diagnostic sessions. The contribution is a mechanism for learning from an expert's evidence-gathering behavior, allowing the sequence of diagnostic actions to influence model refinement as well as the observations those actions produce.
neurips-2011-automated-refinement-of-bay.tldr: Expert choices about diagnostic test order become probabilistic constraints for refining a Bayesian network's parameters.

paragraphs: Some datasets describe relationships through distances between pairs of items. Partitioning such data means using those distances to infer groups. This paper introduces fastTIWD, a Bayesian method inspired by the Translation-Invariant Wishart-Dirichlet process. It retains a probabilistic treatment of clustering, automatic selection of the number of groups, and support for settings with some supervision.

The main change targets computation. In the original method, each Gibbs-sampling iteration requires work proportional to the cube of the number of items. The proposed method reduces this to quadratic work per iteration. This matters because a large collection can make repeated cubic-cost updates particularly expensive, even when the underlying statistical model is attractive.

The experiments show that the reduction in computational cost does not compromise partition quality in the evaluated cases. That is an empirical finding about the resulting groups, alongside the stated reduction in iteration cost. The method makes probabilistic exploration of larger relational datasets more practical while retaining the ability to discover a number of clusters determined through inference.
neurips-2011-bayesian-partitioning-of-la.tldr: fastTIWD reduces Bayesian distance-based clustering from cubic to quadratic work per sampling iteration without sacrificing partition quality in experiments.

paragraphs: A collection of items can have several views, each supplying information that could support clustering on its own. The paper asks how to use those views together. Its starting premise is that the intended cluster assignment for an item should remain the same regardless of which view is used to describe it.

The authors build a spectral clustering framework that encourages agreement between the clustering hypotheses associated with different views. They propose two co-regularization schemes for expressing this consistency requirement. The central idea is to make the views influence one another during clustering, so that the resulting assignments reflect both the available descriptions and their agreement about corresponding items.

Comparisons against several baselines on two synthetic and three real-world datasets support the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. The motivation is that multiple views may yield a more accurate clustering than individual views, and the experiments provide evidence for that hope in the tested settings. The shared-membership premise gives a concrete way to turn multiple descriptions into a coordinated clustering objective.
neurips-2011-co-regularized-multi-view-s.tldr: Two co-regularization schemes improve multi-view spectral clustering by encouraging corresponding items to receive consistent cluster assignments.

paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet Allocation involves hidden topics associated with documents and words. This paper separates several inference tasks within that model and studies their computational difficulty. The distinction matters because finding the most probable word-level topic assignments is a different problem from finding the most probable topic distribution for an entire document.

For word-level assignments, the authors integrate out the document's topic distribution. They show that exact inference takes polynomial time when the effective number of topics per document is small. When a document has many topics, however, finding the maximum a posteriori assignment is NP-hard. Thus, the stated tractability result depends on the document's effective topic count.

The paper then reverses what is integrated out: it removes the word-level assignments and seeks the maximum a posteriori document topic distribution. That task is also NP-hard. Finally, it establishes hardness for posterior sampling in one restricted setting, while leaving the general sampling question open. These results distinguish a tractable regime from several forms of computationally difficult inference.
neurips-2011-complexity-of-inference-in-.tldr: The paper identifies a tractable small-topic regime for LDA inference and proves hardness for several other inference tasks.

paragraphs: A multiclass prediction loss specifies how to penalize a prediction when several labels are possible. This paper studies when such a loss can be understood as two pieces: a proper loss and a link function. Properness connects the loss to truthful probability estimation, while the link provides a way to express predictions in another representation.

The authors extend theory previously developed for binary prediction to the multiclass setting. They characterize stationarity, a Bregman representation, order-sensitivity, and the existence and uniqueness of the composite decomposition. These results address both whether the decomposition is available and what mathematical structure it gives the loss, providing a basis for reasoning about loss design.

The extension also reveals a boundary: the integral representation used for binary proper losses does not carry over to multiclass losses. Separately, the paper relates classification calibration to properness, bringing existing calibration results into its framework. Together, the findings clarify which binary insights generalize and supply theoretical guidance for constructing multiclass prediction objectives.
neurips-2011-composite-multiclass-losses.tldr: The paper characterizes proper composite multiclass losses and shows both how binary loss theory extends and where that extension fails.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction compresses signals into fewer coordinates while trying to retain useful relationships. This paper proposes an unsupervised linear approach grounded in the sparse linear model, which also gives a probabilistic interpretation of sparse coding. Its choice of what to preserve comes from the sparse representation of the signals.

The authors formulate an optimization problem for learning a projection from the original signal space into a lower-dimensional space. The objective is to approximately preserve pairwise inner products in the sparse domain, in expectation. Both qualifications matter: the target is an average preservation property under the model, rather than exact preservation of every pairwise relationship.

The paper derives solutions, introduces nonlinear extensions, and discusses connections to compressed sensing. Experiments use facial images, texture patches, and images representing object categories. Their results suggest that the approach can improve recovery of meaningful structure across several kinds of signals. The contribution is therefore a model-based criterion for compression, together with evidence that preserving sparse-domain relationships can be useful.
neurips-2011-dimensionality-reduction-us.tldr: A learned projection preserves sparse-domain inner products approximately in expectation, with experiments suggesting improved recovery of signal structure.

paragraphs: Paraphrase detection asks whether two sentences express the same meaning. This paper builds a system that compares sentences at both the word and phrase levels. It uses recursive autoencoders to learn feature vectors for phrases organized in syntactic trees, with an unsupervised training objective based on a proposed unfolding construction.

The learned features produce a matrix of similarities between the words and phrases in the two sentences. Because sentence lengths vary, these matrices also vary in size. The authors introduce dynamic pooling to convert each matrix into a representation with a fixed size. This supplies a consistent input format for the classifier that makes the final paraphrase decision.

The method outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches on the MSRP paraphrase corpus in the reported evaluation. Its design connects structured phrase representations with a practical way to compare sentences of different lengths. The autoencoders provide the units being compared, and dynamic pooling makes the collection of comparisons usable by a single classifier across varying sentence pairs.
neurips-2011-dynamic-pooling-and-unfoldi.tldr: Recursive phrase representations and dynamic pooling turn variable-length sentence comparisons into effective paraphrase-classification features.

paragraphs: Simultaneous recordings from many neurons may reveal how a network's activity evolves collectively. This paper asks whether distinct dynamical regimes can be identified directly from those recordings within individual trials. It studies motor cortical activity associated with preparing and initiating hand movements, without using behavioral or experimental epochs to identify the regimes.

The method uses a Hidden Switching Linear Dynamical Systems model. Several linear dynamical laws approximate a process that may be nonlinear and may change over time. Switching between those laws allows the model to segment activity according to its dynamics. The inferred transitions correlate strongly with external events, even when those events occur at different times across trials.

The model also predicts an isolated neuron's firing rate from the others better than recent comparable models. This suggests that it captures more of the variation shared across the recorded population. Together, these findings support the method as a way to trace coordinated network activity whose changes appear related to computation, while preserving the authors' qualified interpretation of that relationship.
neurips-2011-dynamical-segmentation-of-s.tldr: A switching dynamical model identifies single-trial neural regimes that align with external events without using those events to define the regimes.

paragraphs: Generalized linear and single-index models relate a target to a one-dimensional function of a linear predictor. Learning that function and predictor can lead to non-convex estimation. The paper develops efficient learning algorithms by building on Isotron, which alternates perceptron-like predictor updates with isotonic regression, a procedure for fitting a non-decreasing function.

The earlier Isotron guarantee assumed data generated under a generalized linear model, together with monotonicity and bounded-slope conditions, and required fresh samples at every iteration. The authors modify the regression step so that it explicitly fits a function that is both monotonic and Lipschitz, meaning its slope is bounded. They present algorithms described as computationally and statistically efficient.

They also make this constrained regression step faster, reducing its running time from O(n²) to O(n log n). This improvement matters because the step is part of the iterative learning procedure. A brief empirical study demonstrates practical feasibility. The contribution combines a more structured function-fitting step with efficient computation for models whose response depends on a learned linear index.
neurips-2011-efficient-learning-of-gener.tldr: A Lipschitz-constrained isotonic regression step supports efficient learning of generalized linear and single-index models.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene involves more than assigning labels to pixels. This paper jointly addresses three-dimensional layout, three-dimensional objects, two-dimensional faces such as doors and windows, and background segmentation. It represents these elements through a generative stochastic scene grammar that connects scene categories to objects, faces, and lines in a hierarchy.

The grammar uses AND rules to describe parts, OR rules to choose among subtypes, and SET rules to represent collections of entities. Contextual relations express either cooperation, such as alignment or connected faces, or competition, such as mutually exclusive boxes. These structures let the model describe how candidate visual elements can fit together into a scene.

To search the possible configurations, the authors introduce hierarchical cluster sampling, an MCMC inference algorithm. It builds higher-level candidate structures from lower-level elements, then samples alternative structures across the hierarchy to seek the most probable parse tree. The reported public-dataset experiment shows better performance than existing methods, while the resulting parse trees provide richer structural descriptions of the scene.
neurips-2011-image-parsing-with-stochast.tldr: A stochastic scene grammar and hierarchical sampling jointly infer scene layout, objects, faces, and background as a structured parse tree.

paragraphs: Classical sequential prediction can learn a probability distribution over a finite set of outcomes. This paper extends that task to matrices: each observation is an outer product of a unit vector with itself, and the learner seeks a density matrix that explains the sequence. The authors adapt familiar online distribution-learning algorithms to this setting.

A density matrix has many more parameters than a probability vector of the corresponding dimension, so the matrix task appears potentially harder. The central result is that certain adapted algorithms have exactly the same worst-case regret as their classical counterparts. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage relative to the best comparison choice for the observed sequence.

The explanation is that a worst-case sequence of matrix observations shares a common eigensystem, reducing that worst case to the classical situation. Learning the eigenvectors therefore adds no worst-case regret for the algorithms covered by the result. The title's claim of learning them for free concerns this regret comparison, rather than a claim that matrix learning requires no computation.
neurips-2011-learning-eigenvectors-for-f.tldr: Certain online matrix-prediction algorithms learn eigenvectors without increasing worst-case regret relative to their classical distribution-learning counterparts.

paragraphs: A retrieval system may need to select a useful collection of items while learning which collections serve a user well. This paper brings diversified retrieval and online learning into one formulation called linear submodular bandits. The setting supports a general class of utility models with rich features, so the value being learned concerns the selected set.

The authors introduce LSBGREEDY and prove that it converges efficiently to a near-optimal model. The near-optimal qualification is part of the result. This provides a theoretical foundation for learning a model used in diversified retrieval, connecting the ongoing learning process to the quality of the model it approaches.

The case study is personalized news recommendation, where a system selects small sets of articles from tens of thousands available each day. In a live user study, LSBGREEDY significantly outperforms existing online learning approaches. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary questions: whether the learning procedure approaches a strong model efficiently, and whether it benefits an actual recommendation setting.
neurips-2011-linear-submodular-bandits-a.tldr: LSBGREEDY learns diversified retrieval models with a near-optimal convergence guarantee and strong results in a live news-recommendation study.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weak predictors into a stronger prediction rule. This paper develops a multiclass framework using multidimensional codewords and predictors. The authors derive an optimal set of codewords and introduce a loss that encourages a margin, giving the learning objective a way to favor separation between the correct class and competing predictions.

Two algorithms optimize the resulting risk. CD-MCBoost uses coordinate descent to update one predictor component at a time, while GD-MCBoost updates all components jointly through gradient descent. The methods support different weak learners, but share the same broader framework of optimization in a multidimensional space of prediction functions.

Both algorithms are shown to be Bayes consistent, margin enforcing, and convergent to the global minimum of the stated risk. They also become AdaBoost in the two-class case, connecting the framework to binary boosting. Experiments show improvements over previous multiclass boosting methods on several datasets. The paper thus combines a unified theoretical construction with two update strategies and empirical evidence of their effectiveness.
neurips-2011-multiclass-boosting-theory-.tldr: Two multiclass boosting algorithms share consistency, margin, and risk-convergence guarantees while improving on earlier methods in experiments.

paragraphs: Many models of spiking neurons first filter inputs linearly into a low-dimensional signal, then pass that signal through nonlinear stages. This paper proposes a systematic way to estimate the parameters of such cascade models. It addresses both neural mapping from simultaneous excitation of multiple neurons and estimation of sensory neurons' receptive fields.

The method expresses the neuron model as a graphical model and uses generalized approximate message passing, or GAMP, for parameter estimation. GAMP uses Gaussian approximations to loopy belief propagation. In the connectivity application, the method can represent sparsity more accurately and incorporate output nonlinearities, while being computationally efficient. It significantly outperforms earlier compressed-sensing approaches in the reported comparison.

For receptive-field estimation, the same framework can exploit structure in which linear weights are sparse. The authors validate it on linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade models for salamander retinal ganglion cells. The contribution is a shared estimation procedure that accommodates nonlinear neural responses and sparse parameter structure across two related reconstruction tasks.
neurips-2011-neural-reconstruction-with-.tldr: NeuRAMP uses approximate message passing to estimate sparse neural connectivity and receptive fields in nonlinear cascade models.

paragraphs: A single image mixes the appearance of materials with the effects of illumination. Recovering intrinsic images means separating those contributions. This paper approaches that problem through a prior on reflectance: the material-related colors are modeled as coming from a small set of basis colors shared across the image.

The resulting random field model contains global hidden variables for the basis colors while producing reflectance estimates at individual pixels. This links a scene-wide assumption about its color palette to detailed local output. The sparse palette provides information for the separation task that does not depend on detecting and interpreting image edges.

The authors show that their model can produce high-quality results without edge information, comparable to methods that use it. They also report competitive results after adding an edge model. These findings support global reflectance sparsity as a useful source of information for intrinsic-image recovery, and show that it can also be combined with edge-based evidence within the proposed approach.
neurips-2011-recovering-intrinsic-images.tldr: A sparse global palette of reflectance colors helps separate materials from lighting in a single image, even without edge information.

paragraphs: Matrix completion seeks to recover missing entries of a matrix using its known entries and an assumption of low rank. In a recommendation setting, the observed entries can be user ratings for items, and the missing entries are ratings to predict. This paper develops methods for large matrices with most entries unobserved.

The authors use the geometry of the low-rank constraint to reformulate the problem on the Grassmann manifold. This turns the constrained problem into an unconstrained optimization problem on that geometric space. They then apply first- and second-order Riemannian trust-region methods, producing the algorithms RTRMC 1 and RTRMC 2.

Each iteration has a cost linear in the number of observed entries, tying the stated computational workload to the available data. The methods outperform state-of-the-art algorithms across a wide range of tested problem instances. The contribution combines a geometric formulation of low rank with optimization methods suited to that formulation, providing an effective approach to recovering sparsely observed matrices.
neurips-2011-rtrmc-a-riemannian-trust-re.tldr: RTRMC exploits low-rank geometry to complete matrices with trust-region methods whose iteration cost is linear in the number of observed entries.

paragraphs: Training a mixture model on a massive dataset can require repeatedly working with many observations. This paper constructs coresets for Gaussian mixtures and related models. A coreset is a weighted subset designed so that fitting it also gives a good fit to the original dataset, preserving the modeling objective in a much smaller representation.

The central result is that the required coreset size can be independent of the original number of observations. Specifically, the authors show that O(dk³/ε²) weighted points suffice to compute a model within a factor of 1 + ε of the optimum on the original data. The size still depends on dimension, mixture size, and the desired approximation accuracy.

The coresets can be constructed efficiently through map-reduce-style computation or streaming. The theory connects statistical estimation with computational geometry and develops complexity results for Gaussian mixtures. Evaluations include real datasets and density estimation for earthquake detection using mobile-phone accelerometers. The contribution offers a guaranteed compression route for mixture training, alongside construction methods suitable for large data collections.
neurips-2011-scalable-training-of-mixtur.tldr: Gaussian mixture training can use small weighted coresets with approximation guarantees and sizes independent of the full dataset size.

paragraphs: A sparse inverse covariance matrix represents a pattern of relationships in a Gaussian model and can describe the graph of a Gaussian Markov random field. L1-regularized maximum likelihood already has strong statistical guarantees for recovering this structure from limited samples. This paper focuses on making the associated optimization problem easier to solve computationally.

The optimization is a regularized log-determinant program. The authors introduce a Newton-based algorithm that uses a quadratic approximation, incorporating more local information about the objective than a first-order gradient method. They modify the procedure to exploit the particular structure of sparse Gaussian maximum likelihood estimation.

The method is shown to converge superlinearly, and experiments on synthetic and real application data demonstrate considerable performance improvements over other state-of-the-art methods. The statistical estimator supplies the existing motivation for the problem; the paper's contribution is an improved solver for it. Its findings show how adapting second-order optimization to the structure of this estimator can translate into substantial computational benefits.
neurips-2011-sparse-inverse-covariance-m.tldr: A structure-aware Newton algorithm solves sparse inverse-covariance estimation with superlinear convergence and strong experimental performance.

paragraphs: Global optimization can become easier when a large problem can be separated into smaller problems with limited interaction. This paper introduces procedures that discover such a decomposition automatically. They solve the smaller, loosely coupled pieces and use message passing to combine their solutions, bringing methods associated with graphical-model inference into optimization.

The foundation is a new definition of coupling between optimization variables. It generalizes coupling based on expressing a function as terms involving small groups of variables. The framework encompasses statistical independence, sparse Hessian structure, and the generalized distributive law. Despite its greater generality, the authors describe this coupling as easier to check empirically, making the relevant structure easier to estimate.

Experiments show that the proposed methods avoid local minima effectively and obtain better solutions with fewer function evaluations than existing global optimization methods. These are empirical comparisons. The broader contribution is a way to discover exploitable interaction structure and use it to coordinate smaller optimization problems, extending the reach of established inference techniques.
neurips-2011-structure-learning-for-opti.tldr: Automatically learned variable couplings let global optimization problems be decomposed and solved through message passing.

paragraphs: People can judge some members of a collection to be more representative than others. This paper develops a mathematical account of that judgment by extending an existing Bayesian measure. The original measure concerns how representative a sample is of a distribution; the extension asks how representative an individual item is of a set.

The authors establish a formal connection to Bayesian Sets, a machine learning method. Using that connection, they derive an analytic expression for objects represented by sparse binary feature vectors. This makes the proposed psychological measure computable for objects described by a collection of present-or-absent features, linking the theoretical account to a practical representation.

They apply the measure to a large image database to identify representative members of different image sets, then compare its predictions with human judgments. That comparison tests the account using naturalistic stimuli. The abstract does not state the degree of agreement; the reported contribution is the formal measure and its evaluation, demonstrating how image databases can support tests of psychological theories.
neurips-2011-testing-a-bayesian-measure-.tldr: A Bayesian measure of item representativeness is connected to Bayesian Sets and tested against human judgments using image collections.

paragraphs: In linear models, strongly correlated input variables can make L1-regularized parameter estimates unstable. This paper introduces trace Lasso, a penalty that accounts for those correlations when measuring model complexity. The aim is to stabilize estimation by making regularization sensitive to the relationships among the observed covariates.

The penalty uses the trace norm of the selected covariates as a convex surrogate for their rank. Rank reflects how much independent structure a collection of variables contains, so this construction connects the complexity penalty to the design matrix. The authors analyze the norm's properties and describe an optimization algorithm based on reweighted least squares.

Synthetic-data experiments illustrate how the penalty behaves and show that it is better adapted to strong correlations than competing methods such as the elastic net. This supports the proposed correlation-sensitive regularization in the evaluated settings. The main contribution is a model-complexity measure that incorporates the input geometry, together with a fitting procedure and evidence that this adaptation can improve behavior when covariates overlap strongly.
neurips-2011-trace-lasso-a-trace-norm-re.tldr: Trace Lasso uses a correlation-sensitive trace-norm penalty to stabilize linear-model estimation with strongly correlated covariates.

paragraphs: In a palimpsest memory system, storing a new pattern interferes with traces of older patterns. The age of a memory therefore matters for recovering it faithfully. This paper argues that an estimate of age, treated as a form of familiarity, should be closely connected to the neural dynamics that reconstruct the remembered pattern.

The authors investigate this connection using a normative model of autoassociative memory. Their proposed dual system contains interacting modules for familiarity and recollection. The important feature is the interaction: information about a pattern's age is coupled to the process of retrieving it, addressing a relationship the authors say existing theories omit.

Within the model, the dual system gives the best performance for both recollection and recognition. This is a result about the modeled memory system, providing a theoretical reason for distinct but cooperating memory functions. It offers a perspective on psychological and neural debates about recognition by connecting the division of labor to interference caused by storing new memories.
neurips-2011-two-is-better-than-one-dist.tldr: A memory model finds that interacting familiarity and recollection modules best handle retrieval when new memories interfere with old ones.
